by.claim: Auto-sync deploying stale manifests after a hydrator sync-source change is the expected behavior of the hydrator RFC's push-to-stage mode, in which manifests go to the optional `hydrateTo.targetBranch` and "Argo CD relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch" — the deployment branch therefore still holds whatever the promoter last moved, which is exactly the condition the ticket reports observing only in push-to-stage.

The CI `argocd app diff` failures reported in projects that recently enabled the sync impersonation flag are explained by the impersonation design scoping impersonation to the sync path only: the RFC sets Impersonate on the `SyncContext` in the Application Controller's `sync.go` and matches `destinationServiceAccounts` "when executing the kubectl commands for the sync operation", so the server-side-apply dry-run that computes the diff never receives that configuration and runs under a different identity than the sync the reporter is comparing it against.

The delete/re-create loop on a manually deleted ApplicationSet child is explained by the deletion PRD's definition of the `Reverse` deletionOrder, which "Waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next application": a child stuck in Progressing never completes that wait, so the barrier never releases and the controller restarts the wave from the top — a failure mode the PRD does not acknowledge, its Risks and Mitigations section reading "No immediate Risks to consider."

The unbounded `patch` RBAC escalation on external clusters — five rounds of adding resource kinds to the standing cluster credential's ClusterRole — follows directly from the impersonation RFC's implementation list, which names only the GitOps Engine kubectl sync commands and the Application Controller `sync.go` SyncContext as impersonation touchpoints; because Server-Side Diff issues a server-side apply dry-run that Kubernetes authorizes as `patch` against the cluster Secret credential rather than the AppProject's `defaultServiceAccount`, every new resource kind demands real write authority the design never intended to grant.

The hydrator pilot repository's per-push wave behavior in the ProgressiveSync bug is explained by the hydrator RFC's commit model: "Changes originating from a single dry commit are always grouped into a single hydrated commit" on `syncSource.targetBranch`, and "When the application controller detects a new (hydrated) commit on the `syncSource.targetBranch`, it will sync the manifests" — so on a hydrated repo every hydration cycle presents a fresh source change to RollingSync, which is why the pilot is the environment where the spec-only trigger loss surfaces.

The delete/re-create loop on a manually deleted ApplicationSet child is explained by the deletion PRD's definition of the `Reverse` deletionOrder, which "Waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next application": a child stuck in Progressing never completes that wait, so the barrier never releases and the controller restarts the wave from the top — a failure mode the PRD does not acknowledge, its Risks and Mitigations section reading "No immediate Risks to consider."

Auto-sync deploying stale manifests after a hydrator sync-source change is the expected behavior of the hydrator RFC's push-to-stage mode, in which manifests go to the optional `hydrateTo.targetBranch` and "Argo CD relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch" — the deployment branch therefore still holds whatever the promoter last moved, which is exactly the condition the ticket reports observing only in push-to-stage.

The CI `argocd app diff` failures reported in projects that recently enabled the sync impersonation flag are explained by the impersonation design scoping impersonation to the sync path only: the RFC sets Impersonate on the `SyncContext` in the Application Controller's `sync.go` and matches `destinationServiceAccounts` "when executing the kubectl commands for the sync operation", so the server-side-apply dry-run that computes the diff never receives that configuration and runs under a different identity than the sync the reporter is comparing it against.

The commit server pushing unsigned hydrated commits, so that Argo CD rejects its own hydrated output when signature verification is enabled on the hydrated branch, traces to the hydrator RFC's Push access design, which specifies only a `repository-write` Kubernetes Secret carrying GitHub App credentials for the delegated push and raises no signing requirement — its Security Considerations name push permissions, branch protection, and secret placement, never commit signatures.
